|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 341.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 341.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入��式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 341.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 341.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 341.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 341.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 341.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 341.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

## 341.10. Conceptual summary

#+begin summary Section summary
The conceptual chain of this section is:

\[
\text{state vector}
\subset
\text{density operator}
\subset
\text{operator formalism}
\subset
\text{tensor formalism}.
\]

For isomorphism problems, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{isomorphism}
=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.
\]

For complexity theory, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{mathematical encoding}
+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

The main technical danger is confusing a coordinate representation with
the invariant object it represents.
#+end summary

\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 343.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 343.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 343.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 343.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 343.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 343.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 343.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

#+begin summary Section summary
The conceptual chain of this section is:

\[
\text{state vector}
\subset
\text{density operator}
\subset
\text{operator formalism}
\subset
\text{tensor formalism}.
\]

For isomorphism problems, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{isomorphism}
=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.
\]

For complexity theory, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{mathematical encoding}
+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

The main technical danger is confusing a coordinate representation with
the invariant object it represents.
#+end summary

# 344. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 344.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 344.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 345.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 345.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 345.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 345.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

\text{operator formalism}
\subset

=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.

\[

+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

the invariant object it represents.

# 346. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 346.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 346.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 346.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 346.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 347.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 347.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 347.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

\subset

\subset
\text{operator formalism}
\subset

\[
\text{isomorphism}
=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.

For complexity theory, the recurring pattern is:

\[

+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

the invariant object it represents.

# 348. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 348.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 348.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 348.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 348.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 348.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[

=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness

\[

=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 349.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 349.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

=

# 350. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 350.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 350.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 350.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 350.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 350.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 350.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 350.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 350.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python

    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

the invariant object it represents.

# 352. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 352.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

## 352.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 352.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 352.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 352.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 352.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 352.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 352.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 352.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

#+begin summary Section summary
The conceptual chain of this section is:

\[
\text{state vector}
\subset
\text{density operator}
\subset
\text{operator formalism}
\subset
\text{tensor formalism}.
\]

For isomorphism problems, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{isomorphism}
=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.
\]

For complexity theory, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{mathematical encoding}
+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

The main technical danger is confusing a coordinate representation with
the invariant object it represents.
#+end summary

## 354.2. Mixed states and ensemble decompositions

A mixed state represents classical uncertainty over quantum states. Suppose
the system is prepared in state \(|\psi_j\rangle\) with probability \(p_j\).
The probability constraints are

\[
p_j \ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_j p_j = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|.
\]

#+begin important Non-uniqueness of ensemble decompositions
The expression

\[
\rho
=
\sum_j p_j |\psi_j\rangle\langle \psi_j|
\]

does not uniquely determine the ensemble \(\{p_j,|\psi_j\rangle\}_j\).

Different classical preparation procedures may induce the same density
operator. Operationally, the density operator is the object that determines
all measurement statistics.
#+end important

The purity of \(\rho\) is

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2).
\]

In finite dimensions,

\[
\rho \text{ is pure}
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)=1.
\]

A mixed state satisfies

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho^2)<1.
\]

## 354.3. Tensor viewpoint

A bilinear map

\[
\mu : V \times V \to W
\]

can be represented as a tensor

\[
T_\mu \in V^\ast \otimes V^\ast \otimes W.
\]

After choosing bases for \(V\) and \(W\), the map is described by structure
constants \(c_{ab}^k\) satisfying

\[
\mu(e_a,e_b)
=
\sum_k c_{ab}^k f_k.
\]

#+begin define Structure tensor
Let \(V\) and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field \(F\).
The structure tensor associated with a bilinear map \(\mu:V\times V\to W\)
is the tensor \(T_\mu\) whose coordinates are the structure constants of
\(\mu\) in chosen bases.

Changing bases changes the coordinates, but not the abstract tensorial
object.
#+end define

#+begin remark Coordinates versus invariance
Coordinates are useful for computation because they give arrays of field
elements. Invariance is useful for mathematics because it identifies the
features of the object that do not depend on the chosen basis.

中文直觉：坐标是“输入格式”，不变量是“结构本身留下的影子”。
#+end remark

If \(g \in \operatorname{GL}(V)\) and \(h \in \operatorname{GL}(W)\), a change
of basis transforms the structure constants by an expression of the form

\[
c'_{ab}{}^k
=
\sum_{p,q,r}
g_a^p g_b^q (h^{-1})_r^k c_{pq}^r.
\]

This is the source of the orbit formulation of many isomorphism problems.

## 354.4. Isomorphism as an orbit problem

Two tensors \(T\) and \(T'\) are isomorphic if they lie in the same orbit under
a suitable group action. For example, in a three-tensor setting one often
considers an action of

\[
\operatorname{GL}(U)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(V)
\times
\operatorname{GL}(W).
\]

The orbit condition is

\[
T'
=
(g_U,g_V,g_W)\cdot T.
\]

#+begin theorem Orbit formulation
Let \(X\) be a space of encodings of algebraic structures, and let \(G\) be
the group of admissible changes of coordinates. If two encodings represent
isomorphic structures exactly when they differ by a change of coordinates,
then the isomorphism problem is equivalent to deciding whether two points
of \(X\) lie in the same \(G\)-orbit.
#+end theorem

#+begin proof Proof idea
The forward direction says that an isomorphism induces a change of
coordinates. The backward direction says that a valid change of coordinates
preserves the defining structure and therefore gives an isomorphism.

In formulas, the equivalence has the form

\[
A \cong B
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists g \in G
\text{ such that }
g\cdot x_A=x_B.
\]

Thus the classification problem becomes an orbit-membership problem.
#+end proof

## 354.5. Promise problems and reductions

A promise problem is a pair

\[
\Pi
=
(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}},\Pi_{\mathrm{no}})
\]

with

\[
\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}
\cap
\Pi_{\mathrm{no}}
=
\varnothing.
\]

An algorithm for \(\Pi\) only needs to be correct on inputs satisfying the
promise. This differs from a language decision problem, where every string
over the alphabet must be classified.

#+begin define Polynomial-time many-one reduction for promise problems
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be promise problems. A polynomial-time many-one reduction
from \(A\) to \(B\) is a polynomial-time computable function \(f\) such that

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{yes}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{yes}},
\]

and

\[
x \in A_{\mathrm{no}}
\Longrightarrow
f(x)\in B_{\mathrm{no}}.
\]

We write

\[
A \leq_p B.
\]
#+end define

#+begin warning Promise preservation
For promise problems, it is not enough to map yes-instances to yes-instances.
One must also map no-instances to no-instances. Inputs outside the promise
are irrelevant, but the reduction must preserve the promised domain.
#+end warning

A typical reduction chain may have the form

\[
\mathrm{dGA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{GA}.
\]

The tensor analogue might be written as

\[
\mathrm{dTA}
\leq_p
\mathrm{TI}
\leq_p
\mathrm{cTA}.
\]

The point of such notation is not merely symbolic. Each arrow represents
a concrete polynomial-time encoding transformation.

## 354.6. Direct sums and decompositions

Direct-sum decompositions are central in algebraic classification problems.
Suppose

\[
A
=
A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus A_r.
\]

Similarly, suppose

\[
B
=
B_1 \oplus B_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus B_s.
\]

A Krull--Schmidt type uniqueness theorem says that, under suitable
hypotheses, decompositions into indecomposable summands are unique up to
permutation and isomorphism.

#+begin lemma Krull--Schmidt style uniqueness
Assume the ambient category satisfies the Krull--Schmidt hypotheses. If

\[
A
=
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r A_i
\]

and

\[
B
=
\bigoplus_{j=1}^s B_j
\]

are decompositions into indecomposable objects, and if \(A\cong B\), then
\(r=s\) and after a permutation of indices,

\[
A_i \cong B_i
\]

for every \(i\).
#+end lemma

#+begin proof Proof sketch
The proof compares inclusions and projections between summands. By composing
maps around an indecomposable component, one obtains endomorphisms. The
locality of endomorphism rings forces at least one component map to be
invertible. This identifies one matching pair of summands. Removing that
pair and applying induction proves the result.
#+end proof

中文直觉：如果整体分解成不可再拆的小块，那么同构不能把“小块类型”凭空改变，只能重排。

## 354.7. Measurement statistics

Let \(\{M_a\}_a\) be a POVM. The probability of outcome \(a\) in state \(\rho\)
is

\[
p(a)
=
\operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho).
\]

The POVM conditions are

\[
M_a \ge 0
\]

and

\[
\sum_a M_a = I.
\]

Then the probabilities sum to one:

\[
\sum_a p(a)
=
\sum_a \operatorname{tr}(M_a\rho)
=
\operatorname{tr}\left(\left(\sum_a M_a\right)\rho\right)
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)
=
1.
\]

#+begin example Computational basis measurement
For a qubit state \(\rho\), measurement in the computational basis has
measurement operators

\[
M_0 = |0\rangle\langle 0|
\]

and

\[
M_1 = |1\rangle\langle 1|.
\]

The outcome probabilities are

\[
p(0)=\operatorname{tr}(M_0\rho)
\]

and

\[
p(1)=\operatorname{tr}(M_1\rho).
\]
#+end example

## 354.8. Table of recurring structures

| Object | Mathematical form | Computational question | Typical invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure state | vector in Hilbert space | state equivalence | inner product |
| Mixed state | density operator | distinguishability | spectrum |
| Bilinear map | structure tensor | tensor isomorphism | slice rank |
| Graph | adjacency relation | graph isomorphism | degree sequence |
| Algebra | multiplication tensor | algebra isomorphism | radical series |
| Module | representation action | module isomorphism | composition factors |

## 354.9. Algorithmic skeleton

The following pseudocode is not intended to solve tensor isomorphism. It
only gives a schematic form of an invariant-refinement strategy.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, Dict

@dataclass
class Instance:
    name: str
    dimension: int
    data: Any

def coarse_invariants(x: Instance) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "dimension": x.dimension,
        "support_size": len(x.data) if hasattr(x.data, "__len__") else None,
    }

def maybe_isomorphic(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    return coarse_invariants(x) == coarse_invariants(y)

def search_certificate(x: Instance, y: Instance) -> bool:
    if not maybe_isomorphic(x, y):
        return False
    return True
```

## 354.10. Conceptual summary

#+begin summary Section summary
The conceptual chain of this section is:

\[
\text{state vector}
\subset
\text{density operator}
\subset
\text{operator formalism}
\subset
\text{tensor formalism}.
\]

For isomorphism problems, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{isomorphism}
=
\text{same orbit under a group action}.
\]

For complexity theory, the recurring pattern is:

\[
\text{mathematical encoding}
+
\text{polynomial-time transformation}
=
\text{reduction}.
\]

The main technical danger is confusing a coordinate representation with
the invariant object it represents.
#+end summary

# 355. Density Operators, Tensors, and Isomorphism

#+begin summary Section overview
This section discusses a synthetic but mathematically coherent collection
of ideas around density operators, tensor encodings, graph-like reductions,
and algebraic isomorphism problems.

The running theme is that a mathematical object may have several equivalent
representations:

\[
\text{state}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{operator}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{tensor}
\quad \leadsto \quad
\text{orbit under a group action}.
\]

In computational complexity, the representation matters because algorithms
operate on encodings, not on abstract objects directly.
#+end summary

## 355.1. Quantum states and density operators

A pure quantum state is represented by a unit vector \(|\psi\rangle\) in a
Hilbert space \(H\). The normalization condition is

\[
\langle \psi|\psi\rangle = 1.
\]

The corresponding density operator is

\[
\rho_\psi
=
|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|.
\]

This operator is positive semidefinite, Hermitian, trace-one, and idempotent.

\[
\rho_\psi^\dagger = \rho_\psi.
\]

\[
\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\psi)=1.
\]

\[
\rho_\psi^2=\rho_\psi.
\]

#+begin define Density operator
Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. A density operator on \(H\)
is a linear operator

\[
\rho : H \to H
\]

such that

\[
\rho \ge 0,
\qquad
\rho^\dagger = \rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1.
\]
#+end define

#+begin note Positivity and Hermitian structure
In finite-dimensional quantum theory, positivity already implies
self-adjointness. However, listing Hermitian symmetry explicitly is often
pedagogically useful because it reminds us that observables and density
operators belong to the real vector space of Hermitian operators.

中文直觉：正半定保证测量概率非负；迹为一保证总概率为一。
#+end note

The expectation value of an observable \(A\) in state \(\rho\) is

\[
\langle A\rangle
=
\operatorname{tr}(\rho A).
\]

For a pure state, this agrees with the vector-state formula:

\[
\operatorname{tr}(|\psi\rangle\langle \psi|A)
=
\langle \psi|A|\psi\rangle.
\]

\[

A mixed state satisfies
